issues.description: The implementation still enumerates all set partitions (Bell number B_n). For n = 12 this is ~4.2 million partitions and, for the reported failing input, the set of distinct XOR values is expected to contain 4,213,595 entries. Storing that many Python integers in a set and iterating over all partitions will very likely exhaust memory or exceed time limits in typical contest limits. The inspection shows no algorithmic reduction (mathematical/linear-algebraic or DP) to avoid full enumeration, so the solution remains infeasible for the worst-case inputs.

The recursive routine maintains explicit `partitions` lists of indices for each group even though only the group sums (subset_sums) are needed to compute the XOR. Keeping `partitions` increases memory usage and allocation churn unnecessarily and should be removed to reduce overhead.

No automated tests or test harness were provided in the workspace (no unit or integration tests). Acceptance criteria are automatable; a test that reproduces the previously observed TLE case and asserts performance/correctness should be included.

The solution relies on a global set `xor_values` to collect all results; for very large numbers of distinct values this is the main consumer of memory. If the intended correct algorithm produces a large result count (millions), consider whether the problem actually expects printing the count (which is handled) but also whether the environment/time/memory limits make that feasible — include a note or tests to validate resource usage.
